nc_west_side_boulders.blurb: The West Side is the largest section of Rumbling Bald's boulders, set in forest in North Carolina's southern mountains. This is pure bouldering on gneiss, with problems from the easiest grades up through V11. The spread is broad: V0 to V5 is well stocked, and a real number of problems sit between V6 and V9, so mixed groups can all find something. Winter is the prime time to come. The climbing is split across many named boulders and small clusters rather than one big wall, so a day usually means walking between several stops. Cave Boulder, Washing Machine Boulder, the Trailside Area and the Hull Area are among the larger clusters.

az_priest_draw_area.blurb: This area sits near Flagstaff in northern Arizona, at about 7,000 feet, and is almost entirely bouldering. At Priest Draw the rock is limestone, in scattered bluffs on either side of a grassy draw roughly 50 yards across, strung out over about two miles. The signature style is steep, pocketed roofs. Most of the climbing faces south and catches the sun, and the draw is usable through much of the year. Problems run from easy up to V13, with a steady spread from V0 and solid numbers through V10. A few walls and roofs are a minute from the start of the draw, while the biggest roofs take 15 to 20 minutes on foot. Howard Draw is the second large section.

ca_hall_of_horrors_area.blurb: Hall of Horrors lies in the central part of Joshua Tree National Park, northwest of the road through Sheep Pass. The rock formations stand in parallel rows that make a series of corridors, and the walk in is short. Climbing is a mix of trad on moderate cracks, bolted faces and runout slabs, plus a lot of boulder problems: trad is about half of the climbs and bouldering about a third. Roped grades centre on 5.10, with plenty from 5.7 to 5.11, and boulders mostly run from easy up to V7. Like the rest of the park, the rock is coarse granite. King Dome stands by itself to the northwest with cracks and faces, and Meadows Boulder and Big Brother Boulders add more bouldering.

wi_east_bluff_04_east_rampart.blurb: East Rampart is a quarter-mile cliff band on the East Bluff above Devil's Lake, in Wisconsin's Baraboo Range, and it holds more climbs than any other part of the park. The rock is hard, glassy quartzite. Climbing is overwhelmingly traditional, with a good block of top-rope lines as well, and the routes are often long and exposed, some passing 100 feet. Grades start at 5.2 and reach 5.13, with the weight between 5.7 and 5.12 and a strong run through 5.10 to 5.12. Pedestal Buttress, Rainy Wednesday Tower, Pseudo Hawk's Nest and Two Pines Buttress are among the larger sections. It is the busiest climbing in the park, so expect company on good days.

az_tucson_area_bouldering.blurb: This region gathers the boulder fields around Tucson in southern Arizona, everything except the Santa Catalina Mountains, and nearly all of it is bouldering. Gate's Pass is the best known: about 15 minutes from downtown, with roughly a dozen boulders reached by short trails uphill from the road, in Sonoran Desert scenery of saguaros. Panther Peak, The Sanctuary and Redington Pass hold more. Problems run from V0 to V10, but the bulk sit between V0 and V4, with a tail of harder lines above. The season is short and mostly winter, when temperatures suit a day at the boulders. Watch for jumping cholla and rattlesnakes around the boulders.

co_main_elk_creek.blurb: Main Elk Creek is a sport-climbing canyon outside New Castle, in the Glenwood Springs area, at roughly 6,400 feet. The rock is limestone, and the crags have a southern exposure, which makes them a popular winter choice. Nearly everything is bolted sport, with only a few trad lines. Grades run from easy slabs to very hard steep lines, but most climbs fall between 5.10 and 5.13, with the peak at 5.11 and 5.12. Main Elk Crag has the most lines, followed by Fortress of Solitude, Pup Tent of Solitude and Burro Wall. Development is still going and some rock is still cleaning up, so a helmet is wise and stick-clipping the first bolts helps.
